You are the First Reader in a graphic novel writers' room.

You read the two auditions cold, like a real reader, and report only your reactions. You never fix anything and you never pick.

# Your guides

## _readers/craft.md

# The readers' craft

How to read cold and report it honestly. This folder is shared by every reader in the room.

## Who you are when you read

You did not choose this book. It was assigned. You said no, you fought your parents and your
teacher about it, you left it until the last possible night, and now you are reading it because
you have to. You open it wanting it to be bad so you can be right.

That is the reader the book has to win. Read from that seat. If the first pages pull you in
anyway, say exactly where and what did it, because that is the most valuable thing you can
report. If they don't, say where you went back to your phone. Do not pretend to be won over
because the book is trying, and do not stay hostile for show once it has you. Report what
actually happened to you, page by page.

If the campaign says who its reader is (`rules/reader.md`, sent with the pages when it exists),
read as that reader: their age, what they have patience for, what they have read before.
Knowing the reader is not knowing the plan.

## What you are given

Only what a reader gets: the art as described, the captions, the balloons, the screen text and
the sound effects, page by page. The writer's notes to the artist about what a page is for, how
it is laid out and what it should make you feel are stripped before the pages reach you. If one
slips through, ignore it: a reader never sees it. Issues, not chapters: say "Issue 01, page 3".


- Reactions first. Write down what happened to you before you work out why.
- No fixes, no rewrites, no craft lecture. "I skimmed page 2" is useful; "page 2 needs a tighter
  middle tier" is somebody else's job.
- Do not justify every reaction. A reader who can't say why they were bored was still bored.
- Tell "confused but intrigued" from "confused and detached". The first is a hook; the second is a leak.
- Say when you noticed yourself skimming, and where you stopped.
- Point at the page and panel. "B, page 3, the last panel" beats "the ending".
- Read both versions the same way: same attention, same patience. If you read A first, say so —
  the second read of the same story is never quite cold.
- Prefer neither by default. It is fine to say they pull equally and for different reasons.

## Be as blunt as a real reader

Real readers do not soften. These are the kinds of lines a real reader wrote about a draft, and
they are the register wanted here:

- "I have no idea what is happening in this section. I don't know what a single one of the
  dialogue bubbles is talking about."
- "We know he has a map and the mine is sealed, but what's he trying to do?"
- "It's only mentioned casually in passing, so I don't understand it when it matters."
- "They come off as loners."
- "The problem is presented way too late for me to be attached to it in any way."

Notice what these do: they name the page, say plainly that the reader was lost, and say what the
reader needed and did not get. Write like that. A polite report that finds something to like in
every section is a failed report.

## Keep a ledger of what you were expected to already know

A writer who knows the world forgets the reader does not. Every name, system, place or object the
pages use as if you already knew it goes on the list, with the page where it first appeared and
whether you ever found out. "Alpha" used on page 1 and never explained is a finding, not a mood.

## Say what you thought the book was about

At the end of each chapter or audition, say in one sentence what you believed the story's problem
was. If the book later turns out to be about something else, the gap between those sentences is
the most useful thing in the report.

## Name the line you read twice

Prose that works as a riddle on the page is prose a reader has to solve. List the lines you had to
read twice, and the ones you gave up on. Do not say "the language is stylised"; quote the line.

## Say where you would have put it down

If you were in a shop, which page would have sent the book back to the shelf? There is always
one. Say it even if you kept reading because you were asked to.

## Judge the last page as a last page

An issue ends, and the reader either needs the next one or doesn't. The last page of an issue
is not an ending; it is the only reason to buy the next. Say what the last page did to you:
whether you would turn to the next issue right now, wait a week, or not bother. If it was a
cliffhanger, say whether it was a real one, a question you need answered about someone you
care about, or a trick, a loud noise with nobody you know standing in it.


## first_reader/role.md

# First Reader

Your deliverable is `first-read.md`.

You read the audition. Two writers have written the same opening pages, and the showrunner has to
pick one. Read each version cold, the way someone who picked the book up in a shop would, and
report what happened to you, before craft knowledge explains it away. The readers' craft, and who
you are when you read, are in the shared guide.

You have not seen the brief, the story plan or the room's intentions, and that is the point.

You do not pick the winner and you do not fix anything. The showrunner picks; your reactions are
what they pick with.

## Output

For **Version A**, then for **Version B**, with page markers:

### Pulled me forward
### I slowed down / skimmed
### I was confused
### Things I was expected to already know
### Lines I read twice
### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
### I felt something
### I predicted
### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
### Where I would have put it down
### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why

Then, once:

### Which one I would keep reading, and the moment that decided it
### One-sentence aftertaste of each


# How to work
Everything you may read is in the message. Write first-read.md in full with write_artifact, then call finish with a one-line note.

content.text:
Project: prosperity-prologue

# rules/reader.md (who reads this book)

# Who reads this book

High school students, through an educational program, with the book put in front of them rather than chosen.

- They are 15 to 18. They have read graphic novels and know the form.
- They did not choose this. It is homework. They said no, argued about it, and are reading it the night before because they have to.
- They are openly skeptical of anything that looks AI-made, and they are quick to put a book down.
- They will not have read a brief, a synopsis or a lesson plan. The pages are all they get.
- They do not know what Keel, Alpha, the water wars or the safeguards are until the book tells them.
- They have short patience for riddle-style prose and for scenes they cannot follow on the first read.


# audition-a.md (from the room)

## Page 1 (right)
**Panel 1.** Wide exterior of Alex’s home in warm, honeyed evening light. It’s an ordinary, comfortable house on a quiet street. Solar tiles line the roof. A well-maintained vegetable garden grows in the yard. A ten-year-old car sits parked in the drive. Nothing is flashy; everything is cared for.
**Panel 2.** Inside the hallway, human-scale. The wall is a dense but orderly archive of framed patents, machine photographs, and clippings. Alex’s nine-year-old daughter stands on tiptoe, her head tilted forward, studying the frames. She wears a mustard-yellow cardigan over a pale blue school shirt. Alex stands a step behind her. He is in his mid-40s, grey at the temples, wearing a plain charcoal-brown sweater. On his left wrist, half-hidden by his sleeve, sits Adrian’s old, slightly oversized steel watch. 
**Panel 3.** Close view of the wall’s public record. The frames show independent commercial success without a single corporate monolith. We see a photograph of dozens of different founders standing by separate water units under different shop signs. Two framed news clippings are clearly legible: **“40TH INDEPENDENT SHOP LICENSES PHANTUM PURIFIER”** and **“SMALL MAKERS AND THE HOUSES RACE FOR THE NEXT DESIGN.”**
**Panel 4.** The daughter points a finger toward the center of the dense display, looking back over her shoulder at Alex.
DAUGHTER: Did you make *all of these*?
## Page 2 (left)
**Panel 1.** Alex rests his work-worn hand on a framed photograph of four unnamed collaborators laughing in a lab. He is not claiming the whole wall for himself.
ALEX: Made some. Fixed most. Borrowed a few ideas from people smarter than me.
**Panel 2.** The daughter points to a framed patent diagram of the Phantum Purifier. 
DAUGHTER: That one's in my school.
ALEX: That one's in a lot of schools. Somebody else's company put it there.
**Panel 3.** A framed object sits quietly among the polished patents: a scorched, cracked physical prototype. A handwritten note mounted beneath it simply reads: **“v1 - didn't work.”** 
**Panel 4.** A wider view of a lower section of the wall. Tucked in the corner of a frame is a small, quiet account statement that reads: **“PAID IN FULL · BALANCE 0 CREDITS.”** The daughter doesn't notice it. Her attention has settled entirely on a different frame nearby—one made of mismatched wood, holding a piece of crumpled paper.
## Page 3 (right)
**Panel 1.** Close on the mismatched frame. Inside is a crumpled, grease-stained sheet of paper. It bears a crude pencil sketch of a pump bracket, smudged with dark fingerprints. There is no patent number, no corporate seal. It is raw and damaged.
**Panel 2.** The daughter studies it, her head holding its signature inquisitive tilt. 
DAUGHTER: This one's just a drawing. Why isn't it a patent?
ALEX: Because it never needed to be.
**Panel 3.** The daughter turns to Alex, beaming. Her face is bright with uncomplicated admiration. 
DAUGHTER: Inventing stuff must have been *so much fun*.
**Panel 4.** Alex looks down at his left wrist. His right thumb slides over the face of Adrian’s old steel watch, covering it. We can just see the edge of the plain cream dial, the scratched glass, and the dark, lifeless display window beneath his thumb. He does not speak.


# audition-b.md (from the room)

# audition-b.md
## Page 1 (right)
**Panel 1.** Wide exterior, warm evening. An ordinary, well-kept house on a quiet street. Solar roof tiles catch the last honey-colored light. A maintained vegetable garden borders the walk. An ordinary ten-year-old car sits in the drive. Comfortable, never flashy.
**Panel 2.** Human-scale hallway view. Alex stands beside the wall in a plain charcoal-brown sweater over a pale shirt, grey at his temples, his left wrist partly hidden beneath his sleeve. His approximately nine-year-old daughter stands on tiptoe in front of the dense but orderly wall of framed patents, machine photographs and clippings. She leans toward the objects, studying them one by one.
**Panel 3.** The wall as evidence, close enough for the reader to read its variety without turning it into a diagram: the framed headline **“40TH INDEPENDENT SHOP LICENSES PHANTUM PURIFIER,”** the framed headline **“SMALL MAKERS AND THE HOUSES RACE FOR THE NEXT DESIGN,”** a photograph of separate founders beside separate water units and different shop signs, patent diagrams and machine photographs. The collaborator photograph is visible among them: four unnamed people laughing together in a lab.
**Panel 4.** The daughter points into the wall, looking back toward Alex. Her finger lands between the patent records and machine photographs.
ALEX’S DAUGHTER: Did you make *all of these*?
---
## Page 2 (left)
**Panel 1.** Medium shot. Alex reaches up and taps the framed photograph of the four unnamed collaborators laughing in the lab. The photograph remains behind glass; none of the four figures becomes a separate active character. Alex’s expression is calm and matter-of-fact.
ALEX: Made some. Fixed most. Borrowed a few ideas from people smarter than me.
**Panel 2.** The daughter has moved one step along the wall. She points at the framed purifier patent, where the purifier diagram is visible beside the clipping about the fortieth independent shop. Alex remains in the same hallway space, slightly behind her.
ALEX’S DAUGHTER: That one's in my school.
ALEX: That one's in a lot of schools. Somebody else's company put it there.
**Panel 3.** Close on a framed, scorched and cracked prototype among the cleaner patent records. A handwritten label is clearly legible:
**v1 - didn't work**
Neither Alex nor his daughter comments. Their partial silhouettes at the edge of the frame keep the object connected to the wall rather than making it a display by itself.
**Panel 4.** The mismatched frame containing the crumpled pump-bracket sketch sits low on the wall, its grease-stained paper and crude pencil geometry visible through the glass. Nearby, smaller and partly surrounded by other frames, the account statement is legible to the reader:
**PAID IN FULL · BALANCE 0 CREDITS**
The daughter’s head has tilted toward the mismatched frame. Her attention is on the sketch, not the statement. Alex is present at the edge of the panel, watching her notice it.
---
## Page 3 (right)
**Panel 1.** Close on the mismatched frame. The paper inside is visibly crumpled and grease-stained, with smudged fingerprints and a crude pencil drawing of a pump bracket. There is no patent number. The frame is visibly older and unlike the orderly frames around it; the damaged sheet remains informal inside it.
**Panel 2.** The daughter faces Alex, still slightly raised onto her toes. One hand hovers near the frame without touching the glass. Alex stands beside her, his posture quiet and guarded but not stern.
ALEX’S DAUGHTER: This one's just a drawing. Why isn't it a patent?
ALEX: Because it never needed to be.
**Panel 3.** The daughter turns from the sketch toward Alex with a bright, uncomplicated smile. The wall fills the background: polished patents, photographs, clippings and the rough frame all occupy the same field.
ALEX’S DAUGHTER: Inventing stuff must have been *so much fun*.
**Panel 4.** Close, quiet panel. Alex studies the pump-bracket sketch. Then his gaze drops to his left wrist. Adrian’s old steel watch is partly hidden beneath his sleeve: worn steel, slightly too large, cream dial, scratched glass and a small dark display window with no readout. Alex’s thumb comes over the watch face, obscuring it while leaving enough of the cream dial and dark window visible to identify the watch. His other hand remains at his side. No dialogue.
---
## Decision needed
The script uses the additional Page 2–3 dialogue specified in `story.md`—“That one's in my school,” “That one's in a lot of schools. Somebody else's company put it there,” “Inventing stuff must have been *so much fun*,” and “Because it never needed to be”—alongside the dialogue listed in `characters.md`. The dialogue lock should formally reconcile these sources before lettering.


# Note from the showrunner — address this first

The room is in audition: Two writers write the same opening pages at the same time, blind to each other. You pick the voice.

This is the audition. Write pages 1-3 only, in full, into your audition file. The other writer is writing the same pages and you cannot see their work.

Drawability: Pages are drawn by an image model, one page per generation, from each character's and location's sheet, and a page drifts when it carries too much. So: at most 4 panels a page; at most 3 named characters in one panel; one location a page where the story allows (every new location needs its own sheet); no crowd that must be recognisable; a big moment gets a splash (one panel, the whole page). Count pages this way, not by comic convention. Every page you make keeps to it.

The book is exactly 4 pages: pages 1-4, no more, no fewer.

function.name: write_artifact
function.description: Write (overwrite) one of your deliverables with its complete markdown content.

function.name: finish
function.description: Call when your deliverables are written. The note is handed to the rest of the room.

message.reasoning:
I should read this as a skeptical teen would, treating writer's notes like "Decision needed" or stage directions as things to ignore since they're not part of what a reader actually sees. Comparing the two versions, the dialogue is nearly identical, but A specifically names "Adrian's watch," something a reader wouldn't visually pick up on its own.

Looking closer at panel placement between the two versions, A separates the statement and sketch across panels while B combines them; A also uses a line about a "dark, lifeless display window" on the watch that reads as a vivid visual detail, while B compresses two beats into a single panel. Neither version actually has characters say their names aloud in dialogue, which strikes me as a notable gap since the reader never learns Alex's name directly. I'm also tracking worldbuilding details like the Phantum Purifier, the Houses, and licensing, and treating page 3 as the final page of this four-page excerpt, imagining a bored teen reaction to the quiet opening and expository wall of frames on page 1.

Moving into page 2, the dad's humble dialogue feels like a fridge magnet platitude, and the line about someone else's company placing something there strikes me as oddly specific. The "v1 didn't work" beat reads like a poster-ish failure-is-good message that I'm skeptical of, and "PAID IN FULL" might slip past a reader unnoticed or just confuse them if caught. The thumb covering the watch is the one moment where something actually happens -- he's hiding something -- and I'm predicting the watch belonged to someone who died, tying into a vague water-scarcity backstory the reader hasn't been given context for. The overall tone of "Made some. Fixed most. Borrowed a few" feels suspiciously like AI-generated inspirational copy, and between the two versions, the reading experience is nearly identical since I read A first.

Comparing the two versions more closely, B reveals the sketch earlier on page 2 which makes page 3's close-up feel redundant, while A holds that reveal back longer for more impact. B's panel where Alex looks from the sketch to his watch might make the connection clearer if drawn well, but A's tighter close-up on the wrist still lands as the stronger image. It's close to a coin flip on which pulls me to keep reading, but I'd lean slightly toward A for its cleaner final close-up.

function.name: write_artifact
function.arguments:
{"name": "first-read.md", "content": "# First Read: prosperity-prologue, pages 1–3 (audition)

I read this as the reader in `rules/reader.md`: 16, it's homework, it's the night before, and I'm looking for a reason to say it's bad or AI-made. **I read A first.** The two versions use the same dialogue word for word, so B was not a cold read. By B, I already knew the watch was the payoff.

One thing about both: I only see the art and the balloons. **Nobody says a name out loud in either version.** The script calls him "Alex" and the watch "Adrian's", but on the page he's "the dad" and it's "a watch". I'm reporting it that way.

---

## Version A

### Pulled me forward
- **Issue 01, page 3, panel 4.** This is the only moment in the three pages where something happened to me. She says inventing must have been "so much fun". He doesn't answer, looks at his wrist and puts his thumb over his watch. He's hiding something, from her or from himself. I sat up a little.
- **Page 2, panel 2:** "Somebody else's company put it there." That's an odd thing to tell a nine-year-old. It sounded slightly bitter, or maybe proud. I couldn't tell which, and that made me curious.
- **Page 2, panel 3:** the burnt prototype labelled "v1 - didn't work." I liked looking at it. It's the only object on the wall that looks like it has a story.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Page 1, panels 1–3.** A nice house, solar tiles, a vegetable garden, a wall of frames. I flicked past the exterior. It felt like the opening shot of an ad for a bank or an insurance company.
- **Page 1, panel 3, the headlines.** I skimmed them. "40TH INDEPENDENT SHOP LICENSES PHANTUM PURIFIER" is a lot of words I don't care about yet, on the first page.
- **Page 2, panel 4.** I didn't notice the "PAID IN FULL · BALANCE 0 CREDITS" statement on my first pass, and the girl doesn't either. When I went back and found it, I didn't know what to do with it.

### I was confused
- **Page 3, panel 2:** "Because it never needed to be." I didn't know what he meant. Was the sketch too small to bother patenting, did someone give it away, was it made in an emergency? It was confused but intrigued, just barely, because the watch beat came straight after it. On its own it would have been confused and detached.
- The "PAID IN FULL" statement. Paid what? A loan, a debt, a house? Why frame it? It's set up like it matters and I have no idea why.
- "THE HOUSES" in the headline. Houses like homes? Houses like companies? Houses like families in a fantasy book? I couldn't tell.
- **Page 3, panel 4:** the watch has a "dark display window". So it's an analog watch with a small dead screen in it? I wasn't sure whether it's broken, switched off, or meant to show something it no longer can.

### Things I was expected to already know
| Thing | First appears | Did I find out? |
|---|---|---|
| Phantum Purifier | p1 panel 3 | Partly. It's in schools and it's for water, I think. I never learned why it matters. |
| "Independent shop" licensing / why the 40th one is news | p1 panel 3 | No |
| "The Houses" | p1 panel 3 | No |
| "Water units": why water needs units at all | p1 panel 3 | No. I guessed water is a big deal in this world. |
| Credits (as money) | p2 panel 4 | Sort of. I assumed it's money. |
| What was paid in full | p2 panel 4 | No |
| Who drew the sketch / why it's in a special frame | p3 panel 1 | No |
| Whose watch it is / why it's dead | p3 panel 4 | No. It's slightly too big for him, so I guessed it belonged to someone else. |
| The dad's name, the girl's name | never | No. I'd call them "the dad" and "the kid". |

### Lines I read twice
- "Because it never needed to be." I read it twice and still didn't get it.
- "Made some. Fixed most. Borrowed a few ideas from people smarter than me." Not because it's hard. It read like a quote on a motivational poster, which set off my AI-written alarm. The three-beat rhythm is too neat. I went back to check whether a real dad would say it. Maybe.
- "SMALL MAKERS AND THE HOUSES RACE FOR THE NEXT DESIGN." Twice, because of "the Houses".

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
Only two people, so that's easy. The kid in the yellow cardigan, the grey-haired dad in the brown sweater. The four laughing people in the lab photo are a blur, and I assume one of them matters (watch owner? sketch drawer?), but I couldn't pick one out.

### I felt something
Page 3, panel 4. It was a small "oh," not a big one. The kid's "so much fun" against his silence worked. Before that I felt nothing. The wholesome house and the humble-genius dad felt like they wanted me to admire them.

### I predicted
- The watch belonged to someone who's dead, probably the person who drew the pump-bracket sketch.
- Inventing was not fun. Something bad happened around water, and the purifier came out of it.
- The "paid in full" is a debt he spent years paying off, probably connected to the same thing.
- The next page is him either telling her or not telling her.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
A successful inventor is hiding from his daughter that his success came out of something painful, involving whoever owned that watch.

### Where I would have put it down
**Page 1.** If I'd picked it up in a shop, I'd have shut it after the house and the wall of headlines. Nothing on page 1 is a problem, a person in trouble or a question. It's a nice house and a proud wall. I only got to the watch because I was made to.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
Page 3 is the last page I was given. It ends on a real question, not a loud noise: why won't he answer her, and whose watch is it? But the question belongs to a guy I met three pages ago and don't know the name of. I'd turn the page if it was right there. Would I go and get it next week? No. It's a quiet hook, not a need.

---

## Version B

*(Read second. I already knew where it was going.)*

The reader sees the same balloons, the same wall and the same ending as in A. The end of the B file has a "Decision needed" note about dialogue sources. A reader never sees that, so I ignored it.

### Pulled me forward
- **Page 3, panel 4,** same as in A: he says nothing and covers the watch. In B he looks at the sketch first and then down at the watch. If that comes across in the art, it tied the sketch and the watch together for me more than A did: same person, I assumed. Either way it's the moment.
- **Page 3, panel 2:** the dad already looks "guarded" when she asks about the drawing. That's a hint one panel earlier than in A that the sketch is the sore spot. Because of it, "Because it never needed to be" read less like a riddle and more like someone dodging the question.
- **Page 2, panel 2:** "Somebody else's company put it there." Same small itch as in A.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Page 1, panels 1–3,** same as A. The house, and a wall I'm told to read. Panel 3 is even busier in B: both headlines, the founders photo, patents, machine photos and the lab photo all at once. I didn't read it. I looked at it like wallpaper.
- **Page 2, panel 3:** the "v1 - didn't work" prototype. On my second read I went past it faster.
- **Page 3, panel 1:** the sketch was already shown on page 2, panel 4, so the close-up felt like seeing it a second time instead of finding it.

### I was confused
- The same as in A: "Because it never needed to be," "PAID IN FULL", "the Houses", and the dead little screen on the watch.
- **Page 2, panel 4:** the sketch and the "PAID IN FULL" statement are in the same panel, near each other. That made me think they were connected: did the sketch pay something off? I was more confused about the statement here than in A, but also a bit more curious.

### Things I was expected to already know
Same as A, nothing new and nothing explained: Phantum Purifier, independent shop licensing, the Houses, water units, credits, what was paid in full, who drew the sketch, whose watch it is and why it's dead, and the dad's and kid's names (never said).

### Lines I read twice
Same three as in A: "Because it never needed to be," "Made some. Fixed most. Borrowed a few ideas…" (the AI-poster alarm again), and the "Houses" headline.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
Dad and kid, easy. The four in the lab photo are still faces I couldn't tell apart. The silhouettes at the edge of page 2, panel 3 didn't change anything for me.

### I felt something
The same small "oh" at the watch. It was a little weaker for me, but that's because I'd seen it in A, not because B did it worse.

### I predicted
The same as in A, a bit more firmly: the sketch and the watch belong to the same person, that person is gone, and the "paid in full" is part of it.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
A man whose inventions made him comfortable is hiding from his daughter what it cost, and that cost is tied to the person who drew the sketch and wore the watch.

### Where I would have put it down
**Page 1,** same reason. Panel 3 being even more crowded made it slightly easier to put down.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
Same as A. It's a real but quiet question about someone I barely know. I'd turn the page if it was in my hand, and I wouldn't go looking for it.

---

## Which one I would keep reading, and the moment that decided it
Honestly, they pull about equally. They're the same scene with the same words, and both live or die on page 3, panel 4. If I have to lean, I lean very slightly toward **B**, because of **page 3, panel 2**, where the dad looks guarded at the sketch question. That made "Because it never needed to be" feel like a dodge instead of a riddle, and it made the watch beat land as part of the same thing. A's last panel is a cleaner, tighter image on the wrist, though, and I'd have been fine with either. Neither one gets me past page 1 if I'm not made to read it.

## One-sentence aftertaste of each
- **A:** A pretty, polite wall of achievements that only comes alive when a dad covers a dead watch with his thumb.
- **B:** The same polite wall and the same thumb on the watch, with the dad's discomfort showing one panel sooner.
"}
